articles.title: Canada raises study permit funds requirement to CAD 23,448 from Sept 1
articles.summary: Rest of World News: International students applying for a Canadian study permit from Sept 1, 2026 will have to demonstrate that they have at least Canadian dollars (CAD) .
articles.body: International students applying for a Canadian study permit from Sept 1, 2026 will have to demonstrate that they have at least Canadian dollars (CAD) 23,448 available for living expenses (if they are headed to a province or territory other than Quebec).The amount is in addition to tuition fees and transportation costs. The requirement applies to the student as well as any accompanying family members, with the amount increasing according to family size.The new threshold represents an increase from the current requirement of CAD 22,895, applicable to applications made between Jan 1, 2025 and Aug 31, 2026.The change is part of Canada's annual adjustment of the financial requirement for international students. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) states that the amounts are updated each year.From CAD 10,000 to CAD 23,448 in three yearsWhile the latest increase is relatively modest, the financial requirement has changed substantially over the past few years. Until the end of 2023, students were required to demonstrate CAD 10,000 for living expenses. In January 2024, the requirement was more than doubled to CAD 20,635 to meet rising costs especially those related to housing. It has subsequently been adjusted upwards each year.Gurpreet Oshan, a regulated Canadian immigration consultant (RCIC), says the September 2026 increase should be viewed in the context of this broader change. “The increase taking effect on Sept 1, 2026, should be understood as part of Canada’s annual adjustment of the financial requirement for international students, rather than as a standalone policy restriction.”For a single student, the requirement rises from CAD 22,895 to CAD 23,448. “While the increase this year is relatively modest, the larger shift in Canada’s international student policy is significant. Until 2023, students were required to demonstrate only CAD 10,000 for living expenses, a figure that had become completely disconnected from the actual cost of living in Canada. The government substantially increased the requirement in 2024 and has since moved to annual adjustments based on cost-of-living data, Oshan says.How much money will students need to show?For applications made on or after Sept 1, 2026, the following amounts apply to all provinces and territories except Quebec.Number of family members, including applicantLiving expenses required per year (In CAD)123,448229,192335,888443,572549,419655,736762,054Each additional family member6,318These amounts are for living expenses only and do not include tuition or transportation costs.For example, a student travelling to a province other than Quebec with two family members would have to show CAD 35,888 for living expenses for one year. Tuition and transportation costs would have to be demonstrated separately.How the requirement has changedApplication periodOne studentIncrease byUntil 2023CAD 10,000—From January 2024CAD 20,635More than doubledJanuary 2025–August 2026CAD 22,895CAD 2,260From September 1, 2026CAD 23,448CAD 553The minimum balance is not the only considerationFor prospective students and their families, meeting the prescribed amount should not be seen as sufficient by itself. IRCC says applicants must prove that they have enough money, without working in Canada, to pay for tuition, living expenses for themselves and accompanying family members, and transportation to and from Canada.Applicants have to demonstrate that they have sufficient financial resources for the first year of their studies. If the programme is longer than one year, they must also explain how they intend to finance the full duration of their studies.Oshan says this is an important distinction for applicants. “Meeting the minimum dollar figure does not automatically establish financial capacity. Immigration officers assess the source, availability and sustainability of the funds, and for programs longer than one year, applicants are also expected to demonstrate how they intend to finance the remainder of their studies.”In other words, applicants need to demonstrate not just that the required money exists, but that the financial plan supporting their education and stay in Canada is credible.What can students use as proof of funds?IRCC lists a range of documents that can be used to demonstrate financial capacity. It says the list is not exhaustive, and applicants do not necessarily need to provide every document listed. They need to provide sufficient evidence to establish that they meet the financial requirements.Some examples include:Source of fundsExamples of supporting documentsTuition and study costsProof that first-year tuition and housing fees have been paid; student or education loanScholarshipsProof of scholarship or participation in a Government of Canada-funded educational programmeEmployment incomeRecent pay stubsFinancial support from another person/institutionSupport letter, evidence of the sponsor's employment or occupation, relationship to applicant and amount of supportCanadian bank accountProof of a Canadian bank account in the student's nameInvestmentsGuaranteed Investment Certificate (GIC) from a Canadian financial institutionBank savingsBank statements for Canadian or foreign accounts for the past six monthsOther incomePension-plan documents or proof of rental incomeIRCC says bank statements should cover the past six months, including the month the application was submitted or the month immediately before it. Documentation showing the source of income — such as employment income or savings transfers — should accompany the statements.Where a student is being financially supported by another person, documentation should establish the relationship between the applicant and the person providing the money, as well as the nature and extent of the support. The supporting documentation may include the sponsor's employment information, pay stubs and identification or business-registration evidence.Paying tuition upfront does not replace proof of living expensesStudents who have already paid their first-year tuition and housing fees can use the receipt as part of their financial documentation. However, IRCC makes clear that this must be accompanied by other evidence showing that the student has sufficient funds for living expenses and transportation.Similarly, if a scholarship covers tuition but not living expenses, the applicant has to provide additional evidence demonstrating sufficient funds for those expenses.Financial planning becomes more importantFor Indian families in particular, Oshan says the new requirement reinforces the need to plan finances well before the study-permit application is submitted.“For Indian families planning Canadian education, this means financial planning needs to happen much earlier. The question is no longer simply whether a family can arrange enough money to meet a minimum balance at the time of application.”Instead, families need to be prepared to demonstrate how the student's education and stay will be financed. “They need to be able to demonstrate a credible and sustainable financial plan for the student’s education and stay in Canada. The higher threshold could make Canada less accessible to some students, although it also brings the immigration requirement closer to the economic reality students face once they arrive,” says Oshan.What about students going to Quebec?IRCC notes that Quebec establishes its own cost-of-living threshold for international students seeking to study at educational institutions in the province. Applicants seeking a Quebec Acceptance Certificate (CAQ) must demonstrate that they can financially cover the costs specified by Quebec's Ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration.Therefore, students planning to study in Quebec need to meet the applicable Quebec financial requirements rather than relying on the federal figures for other provinces and territories.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: At least seven dead after ferry capsizes off Northern Cyprus
articles.summary: Northern Cyprus Prime Minister Unal Ustel says 237 people rescued and 23 people remain missing.
articles.body:
At least seven people have died after a boat with more than 260 people on ⁠board capsized off the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus on Sunday, Turkish media reported.

Northern Cyprus Prime Minister Unal Ustel said that at least seven people died after the ferry capsized, CNN Turk reported on Sunday, adding that 237 others had been rescued and 23 people remained missing.

“There has been a huge deployment to the area as part of the search-and-rescue effort affiliated with the Northern Cyprus Coast Guard Command,” Al Jazeera correspondent Resul Serdar said.

The Coast Guard Command deployed passenger ships, five pilotage units, and two coast guard helicopters. The Turkish Naval Forces assigned another six naval units.

The catamaran-style vessel had left the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, and started sinking a few kilometres off the coast.

Ustel said that a total of 267 people, including the crew, had been on board the vessel when it capsized.

Northern Cyprus Transport Minister Erhan Arikli told Turkish news agency Anadolu that a rescue operation was under way to bring any injured people to Girne port and then transfer them to local hospitals.

Arikli added that the cause of the incident would be investigated.

“What we know is that a privately operated passenger ferry, a catamaran, departed the port of Girne at around 12:30pm local time [09:30 GMT] for Tasucu port in Turkiye’s southern city of Mersin, and began taking on water for an as-yet-unknown reason shortly after leaving the port,” Serdar reported.

The captain issued a distress call as the ferry began taking water, prompting the Coast Guard and port authorities to dispatch rescue teams to the area.

Images broadcast by Turkish television showed the upside-down ferry in the water, with people wearing life vests atop its orange hull. The weather was sunny, and several boats were seen in the area to lend assistance.

“All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services,” the Ministry of Health of Northern Cyprus said in a statement.

It added that hospitals in the territory had been alerted, so they could provide any medical attention that might be needed.

articles.title: Seven killed and 23 missing in boat capsizing off northern Cyprus
articles.summary: A search and rescue operation is under way after a ferry carrying nearly 270 people turns over after leaving port.
articles.body:
Seven people have died and 23 others are still missing after a passenger boat capsized off northern Cyprus, the head of the Turkish administration there has said.

Ünal Üstel, the prime minister of the self-proclaimed territory, which is only recognised by Turkey, said the ferry ha been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members when it began taking on water after departing the coastal town of Kyrenia.

He offered his condolences to the families of those who had died, wishing them "patience and strength".

A search and rescue operation to find the passengers still unaccounted for is under way.

The privately owned ferry left the port at 12:30 local time (09:30 GMT), local media report.

Helicopters and coastguard boats have been dispatched to the scene, while ambulances have been stationed on the beach ready to receive rescued passengers.

Üstel wrote on social media that the "priority right now is human life", adding that security forces, rescue teams and health officials were all on the scene.

The transport minister of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), Erhan Arikli, told local media that 100 passengers had been taken to shore.

The Filo Jet vessel is a high-speed 40m long and 10m wide craft that sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic.

Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident".

A hotline has been set up to provide passengers' relatives with information.

Local television has broadcast images of the upside-down ferry in the water, with people wearing life vests atop its hull.

The TRNC, which is recognised only by Turkey, controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.

articles.title: Welsh bushcraft expert competes on Alone: World Championship
articles.summary: Andrew Price says the bitterly cold temperatures were the hardest part of the challenge.
articles.body:
Dropped in the Arctic Circle with just 10 tools and a camera, Andrew Price faced loneliness and lit fires to cook and boil water.

Despite worries of grizzly bears and the extreme cold, the 51-year-old has become the first Welshman to compete in the US TV show Alone: World Championship.

"I've always wanted to push myself in a really cold environment, it doesn't get colder than the Arctic Circle so it felt like the perfect place to go," Price said.

"It was definitely the most physically and mentally challenging thing I've ever done."

Growing up in the suburbs of Swansea, Price's grandad introduced him to foraging for seaweed, mussels and blackberries on the Gower Peninsula.

When he was eight, his grandad used to take him on walks in Mumbles to collect periwinkles and boil them for food.

"As a kid, it seemed like a normal thing to do but only later on in life that I realised not everyone did that," Price said.

With his dad, he used to go out kayaking and fishing around Mumbles Head, trying to catch mackerel and bass.

This later introduced him to bushcraft, which includes skills such as hunting in a natural environment.

After leaving school, Price went on an expedition to Malaysia where he spent several months living with the indigenous people of Peninsular Malaysia, Orang Asli.

He described the experience as "very immersive" as he learned what it was like to live in a jungle and hunt with blowpipes.

It exposed him to a society living sustainably from the land.

Before returning to Wales, Price travelled the world to learn more about different landscapes and cultures.

"I'd done things that made me think there was a lot more to do in the world than just sort of working in Swansea," he said.

At the time, bushcraft was not recognised as a career path but Price decided to share his knowledge with others.

In 2004, he began teaching bushcraft, using it as a tool to support people with anxiety and depression.

"People learn real tangible skills, and with that there comes a lot of self confidence," he said

Price also spent seven years co-hosting the Bafta-nominated ITV Wales series Coast and Country.

In 2015, Price first applied to go on Alone but it was only open to Canadians and Americans, until the first ever international season this year.

"I was at a point in my life where I didn't have much going on as my daughter was getting a bit older," he said.

Representing Wales, he got the opportunity to bring in many Welsh traditions and felt keen to be represented as a Welsh person rather than just a British person, in the competition to win $500,000 (£367,000)

"We're known for rugby, music and poetry, but not necessarily for survival skills," Price said.

He was left to be on his own for a long time in the show, which he found was a difficult thing to do.

"What makes Alone so special is it allows you to push yourself to the absolute limit.

"You are only in competition with yourself.

"It can be a massive challenge but that's the beauty of it."

Every survivalist was given a GPS tracker where a helicopter could pick them up if they couldn't go any further.

Knowing there were grizzly bears and having no access to technology made it seem more extreme to Price's family.

But he felt the environment was the hardest part, especially with the temperature drops and staying motivated.

He said being able to light fires for cooking and boiling water was the most useful skill.

"I learned that I could tolerate more than I thought possible," said Price.

"I've become a much more patient and hopefully better instructor as a result of going on Alone."

The 13th series of the show premiered on Sky History involving 10 survivalists from seven countries including Wales, the US, Canada, Australia, Slovenia, Portugal and New Zealand.

articles.title: Death toll from Russian strike on Ukrainian arms depot rises to 38
articles.summary: Russia’s Defence Ministry announces plans to launch ‘massive strikes’ against Ukraine’s infrastructure before winter.
articles.body:
The death toll from a Russian strike on an arms depot near the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, has risen to 38, marking the war’s deadliest attack so far this year, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Emergency workers on Sunday continued to extinguish the resulting fires and explosions that began on Saturday in the village of Myla, Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram, adding that bomb disposal teams were also working to clear the site.

He said 20 people were injured, while four remained missing.

The attack was the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv within two months, with officials voicing anger that arms were still being stored so close to residential areas.

Ukrainian prosecutors have opened an investigation into alleged criminal negligence.

Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces were preparing to launch “massive strikes” against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, following a Ukrainian drone campaign against Wildberries , dubbed “Russia’s Amazon”, as well as the country’s oil and gas sector, which Kyiv says both funds and directly fuels Moscow’s war in Ukraine.

During the war’s previous winters, Russia systematically battered Ukraine’s power grid, depriving thousands of heat and light in freezing temperatures . Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that the coming winter may prove the most challenging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Ukrainian military said it launched overnight attacks on an oil refinery in Russia’s Leningrad region and a military base in the Krasnodar region.

One person was killed in a separate Ukrainian attack on a mine in the Russian-controlled part of the Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine, Moscow-installed Governor Leonid Pasechnik said.

United States-led diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, Europe’s deadliest since World War II, have been at a standstill for months.

Russia has demanded sweeping territorial and political concessions from Ukraine, which Kyiv has ruled out as tantamount to capitulation.

articles.title: These men had a hellish escape from Nepal’s flooded hydro tunnels. They were the lucky ones
articles.summary: As water, concrete and debris stormed through the darkness, almost sweeping him off his feet, Ram Chandra tightly gripped onto one of the rungs studded into the roof of the tunnel he was working in on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli river.
articles.body: As water, concrete and debris stormed through the darkness, almost sweeping him off his feet, Ram Chandra tightly gripped onto one of the rungs studded into the roof of the tunnel he was working in on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli river. His quick reaction likely saved his life. He and the small group of colleagues he was with were hundreds of meters from the exit. “The water was rising and it was difficult to move my legs. If I had let go from that rung I would have fallen.” He grabbed hold of a tin sheet to have something to place under his feet and they passed it around the group as they inched their way forward rung, by rung for six hours. “There were six of us and we later found someone else at the gate of the tunnel,” he said. By the time they emerged, the waters had claimed their clothing. In the daylight they saw the catastrophic destruction the flood had left in its wake, the still surging river below, stained dark by the debris, ice and silt. The mountains above had unleashed a cataclysmic, deluge that swept 62 miles (100 km) downstream, killing hundreds and burying entire communities in the worst natural disaster to hit Nepal in years. Among the missing, are more than 900 workers, like Chandra from the many hydropower projects that bore deep into the world’s highest mountain range to tap into the fearsome energy unleashed by its raging rivers. Some 279 hydro power workers have been rescued, or managed to trudge their way out of the mud and silt riddled tunnels. But others are feared trapped. At the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant, searchers worked through the night into Sunday boring a hole to pump in air and drop down food –– in the hope of making contact with anyone who might be trapped in the tunnel there. Survivors a minority Madan Singh Budha had come off the night shift at the Upper Trishuli tunnel number 2 when the deluge struck. “When I looked outside, I could see water and so I started running up the hill,” he told CNN after being brought down from the disaster zone by helicopter on Sunday. “The hill was rocky, with grass growing in between. We used that grass to hold on to as we climbed.” “Those who weren’t able to climb up were swept away.” Then began the desperate, confusing search for their colleagues. Madan Singh Budha, Ram Chandra and roughly 15 other rescued hydro workers CNN spoke to hail from Jumla in the far west of Nepal — a region of maize terraces clinging to steep mountainsides and close-knit village communities that seems a world away from where the disaster struck. Everyone in the group had lost a relative or friend. Like Chandra, many had even lost their clothes to the torrent, and were attired in borrowed trousers, shirts and sandals, lent by villagers when they had scrambled to safety. Bhakti Ram Bohara is one of the survivors. By his account, he is in a minority. He estimated there were about 1000 people working on his and other nearby projects. Only around 100 of those had made it out. Among the missing was his brother-in-law. They worked with on the same team, spending weeks away from their families at a time, and sending money back to their home villages. “His wife is my sister, and she is pregnant,” he said, breaking down into tears. ‘No one wants to go back there’ Amar Bista, a tour guide, was not working at the tunnels but rushed into action as soon as he heard of the catastrophe at the site, where dozens of his family members and friends worked. Finding out who was missing and who was safe, and then bringing them out had been a near impossible task. He hadn’t slept for four days, he told CNN, standing with the group he had help save. “They all are from my area, you know,” he said through tears, gesturing to the men standing silently around him. When he reached the site by helicopter, the scale of the disaster hit him hard. “People still have hope,” he said, referring to media reports of people being rescued from the worst affected areas. “But the reality is nothing.” “A lot of nights I cannot sleep (because I’m) crying. You know, like some of my cousins, sisters, they lost their kids. You can only imagine, like 18 year kids,” he said. As he spoke, a constant stream of military and civilian helicopters roared overhead on the seemingly ceaseless task of bringing out survivors and the dead. He said he was grateful for the work of the authorities. Up at the disaster site, the rescue required something almost unthinkable: going back into the tunnels that had claimed so many of his people. “No one wants to go back there,” he said. “But they want their friends back.” Late on Sunday the group filed onto a bus that would take them back to the capital Kathmandu, the first step in a journey back to Jumla and their families that can take days by road. “We want people to know we tried our best to bring our friends back,” Amar said, his voice wavering. “Even the dead body.”

articles.title: In 2021, Amazon shut down its US rooftop solar systems after six critical incidents across 47 North American solar sites; a later global audit found 259 major issues
articles.summary: US News: Rooftop solar systems are designed to produce electricity for years, but problems in their wiring and connections can create serious safety risks. Ama.
articles.body: Rooftop solar systems are designed to produce electricity for years, but problems in their wiring and connections can create serious safety risks. Amazon faced this issue at several of its facilities in North America between April 2020 and June 2021, when six solar sites reported critical fire or arc flash events.Amazon had solar installations at 47 North American sites. Six of them experienced either a fire or an arc flash event during the 14-month period. This meant that about 12.7% of the sites with solar installations were affected.The incidents included a three-alarm fire at an Amazon fulfilment centre in Fresno, California, on April 14, 2020. The fire damaged 220 solar modules. Fourteen months later, a two-alarm fire at a facility in Perryville, Maryland, brought around 60 firefighters to the site.The incidents led Amazon to take its US solar operations offline by June 2021. The company wanted the systems to be properly designed, installed and maintained before they were switched back on. According to Eco portal, an internal Amazon report described the rate of dangerous incidents as “unacceptable and above industry averages”.What caused problemsAmazon brought in Clean Energy Associates (CEA), an outside inspection firm, to examine its rooftop solar portfolio. The audit found one critical issue and 259 significant findings across sites in the US, Asia Pacific and Europe, Middle East and Africa.The findings included mismatched module-to-module connectors, incorrectly installed connectors, poor wire management and signs of water entering inverters. These were not defects in the solar panels themselves. Instead, many of the problems were linked to how the different parts of the systems had been connected or installed.Connectors are important because they join electrical cables and allow electricity to move between different parts of a solar system. If two connectors do not fit properly, electrical resistance can develop at the connection.Resistance can produce heat. As the connection becomes hotter, the plastic around it can soften, which can make the connection even less secure. In some cases, this can lead to an electrical arc.Solar systems also have a particular safety challenge because they generate direct current, or DC. Unlike household alternating current, or AC, direct current flows continuously in one direction.In an AC system, the current repeatedly passes through zero. This can help an electrical arc stop. A solar circuit, however, can continue supplying current while sunlight is available, allowing an arc to keep burning.Why connectors became major concernLarge commercial solar arrays contain thousands of electrical connections. Every solar module has electrical leads, while larger systems can have additional connections for components such as optimisers and microinverters.These connections remain exposed to outdoor conditions for years. They have to withstand repeated heating and cooling, rain and strong sunlight while remaining secure.Another problem can occur when connectors made by different manufacturers are used together. They may look similar and fit physically, but that does not necessarily mean they have been tested to work safely together.Amazon's audit identified mismatched connectors and connectors that had been installed incorrectly among its major findings. Poor wire management was another concern. A cable that is not secured properly can move against other parts of the system over a long period, potentially damaging the cable.Water intrusion was also found in some inverters. Inverters are devices that convert the DC electricity produced by solar panels into alternating current that can be used by electrical systems.The cost of keeping the systems offlineThe solar incidents also created financial costs for Amazon. According to the internal documents, each event cost an average of about $2.7 million.Amazon's divisions requested $3.6 million in late 2021 to reinspect sites where significant findings had been reported. Internal teams also pushed the company to use more salaried employees for solar operations instead of depending heavily on outside vendors.Keeping the 47 North American solar sites offline also meant lost electricity generation. The documents estimated the loss at about $940,000 per month, or around $20,000 per site.The problems also came as safety requirements for solar connectors were being tightened. The 2020 wiring code added a requirement that connectors used together must be listed and identified as being suitable for intermatability when they are not the same type and brand.However, that change applied to installations covered by the updated code. Older systems were not automatically required to be inspected again under the new requirement.By the end of 2021, Amazon had rooftop solar powering 115 of its fulfilment centres globally.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: USS George Washington captain says morale is high for new Mideast mission
articles.summary: Ship's commanding office says morale is high on the USS George Washington as it replaces the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Morale is said to be high as the aircraft carrier the USS George Washington has arrived in the Arabian Sea near the vital Strait of Hormuz and close to Iran. The carrier, CVN 73, has replaced the USS Abraham Lincoln. Fresh from a visit to Vietnam three weeks ago, the 5,000 sailors aboard this mobile airfield, base to approximately nine operational squadrons of advanced strike fighters, electronic attack planes and helicopter assets are, according to senior officers, ready and willing to carry out their new mission. "Morale aboard USS George Washington remains high among our sailors," Capt. Nicholas DeLeo, the ship’s Commanding Officer, told Fox News Digital. He added "I see this as I walk the deck plates, seeing them take pride in their work — whether conducting flight operations, maintaining our systems or supporting one another on the ship. The dedication and teamwork I see across the ship is outstanding, and that spirit keeps us ready and resilient." CENTCOM COMMANDER TOUTS USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN MENTAL HEALTH RECORD AFTER MORE THAN 260 DAYS WITHOUT PORT CALL The George Washington, a Nimitz-class carrier, is the flagship of Carrier Strike Group (CSG) 5, and is reported to be accompanied by several warships, including the guided missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls (CG 62) and the guided missile destroyer USS Shoup (DDG 86). Commander of Carrier Strike Group Five, Rear Adm. Jeff Heames, told Fox News Digital "The teams aboard USS George Washington and Carrier Strike Group Five are ready, determined, and resourced for sustained operations. Our Sailors understand the importance of the mission and continue to execute with precision and professionalism every day." With the carrier group now operating in the Middle East, it falls under US Central Command (CENTCOM). The command’s former Commander, Gen. Joseph Votel, (Ret.), recently told Fox News’ America Reports about the George Washington’s expected mission, saying "Being able to continue to have credible military capability in the Middle East is really important, so the arrival of the George Washington is I think a good example of that." Votel continued, "We’re going to have to be prepared, because this is probably going to take some time, to continue to bring forces into the region, we want them to be at a high level of readiness." IRAN WAR THRUSTS DIEGO GARCIA INTO SPOTLIGHT AS OFFICIAL CALLS US MILITARY BASE ‘INTEGRAL’ Flight operations continue, both day and night. Launching into the skies off Iran from the George Washington, aircraft based on board are reported to be F/A-18E/F Super Hornet multirole strike fighters, F-35C Lightning II fifth-generation stealth multirole fighters, EA-18G Growler electronic warfare aircraft and E-2D Advanced Hawkeye airborne early warning and control. Also onboard are said to be MH-60S Seahawk & MH-60R Seahawk multi-mission helicopters for anti-submarine warfare and search-and-rescue. This past week, a historic landing on the George Washington. Navy Lt. Steven Frazier, a pilot from Strike Fighter Squadron 147, the Argonauts, made the 200,000th trap - landing on the ship in an F-35C Lightning II fighter jet, with his stealth fighter caught by a thick, steel arresting gear cable with the jet’s tail hook. In a laid-back understatement that could have come straight out of the movie ‘Top Gun’, Lt. Frazier said, "It's a good feeling for me to know that once I leave, I can come back to the aircraft carrier and trap". The carrier can land one aircraft on deck per minute, and typically lands 70 aircraft a day. IRAN WAR FORCES AMERICA TO CONFRONT THE STRATEGIC COST OF DETERRING CHINA Attention to mission is evident throughout the ship. On the bridge, Assistant Navigator Elizabeth Wayne told the ship’s communication team, "all of the time when we are navigating, we are focused outside of the ship on anything that could pose a hazard or a threat to the ship." Wayne continued, "When we are in special evolution, when we are conducting flight operations, the most important thing is to ensure we are lock step with (the) airboss, the captain, the command duty officer underway, everybody needs to be on the same page to execute that safely." As it arrived in the Middle East, Russia tried to suggest the food on the carrier was not good. Russia Today (RT) posted what are believed to be AI-generated photos of poor rations on board. However, from the videos seen by Fox News Digital of great food and even a café below decks, the truth appears to be very different. Victoria Marc, Culinary Specialist 2nd Class, talked to the communications team on the carrier, noting that "throughout the day and into the night, our sailors have all sorts of food and drink options available to them." Marc added, "Sailors have the opportunity to eat three meals a day, plus the night rations. Our 150 cooks work 24 hours to prepare and serve 15,000 meals a day to ensure our sailors are well-fed. From the mess deck throughout the day, there’s always something there where people feel fueled and ready for the fight." And the Navy intends keeping it this way. Earlier this week, CENTCOM published images of the George Washington being replenished at sea. Navy images show the ship being resupplied twice in four days this past week, an average of 2,000 pallets of supplies including fresh food and ammunition winched by helicopter from a nearby supply ship. Fuel for the carrier’s aircraft is also transferred ship-to-ship. The carrier is nuclear-powered, so the ship itself will not need refueling at sea. WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS More history this week – under the headline "Shoutout to our Shipbuilders!!", the ship’s communications team posted "40 years ago on August 25, 1986, the keel for USS George Washington was laid." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Today in the Arabian Sea, that keel supports the 5,000 men and women and their array of air firepower, as they stand at the coalface of the Middle East conflict, ready – and willing – to carry out their mission.

articles.title: Dungannon: Child in 'critical' condition as police continue murder investigation
articles.summary: A male who was arrested on suspicion of murder and attempted murder remains in custody.
articles.body:
A child remains in a critical condition and a murder investigation under way following an incident at a house in Dungannon .

Police say the body of a man was found alongside the injured child, understood to be a girl, at a property in Lisnahull Road at about 11:00 BST on Saturday.

A woman who had sustained non-life threatening injuries during the incident has been released from hospital.

A male who was arrested on suspicion of murder and attempted murder remains in custody.

"The cause of the man's death has not yet been formally established and post-mortem examinations will take place in due course," Det Ch Insp Robinson of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) added.

"As such, it would be inappropriate to comment further and I would ask that the public avoid speculation until we can provide further updates.

"However, I want to reassure the public that we do not believe that there is any ongoing risk, and at this stage we are not seeking anyone else in relation to the deaths.

"Our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of those involved."

BBC News NI understands the man who died was from Guinea-Bissau, but had lived in Northern Ireland for more than two decades.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) said they received a 999 call at 11:08 BST on Saturday, following reports of an incident.

They dispatched a helicopter crew, three emergency crews, one advanced care paramedic, two ambulance officers and one HART (Hazardous Area Response Team) crew to the scene.

Sinn Féin assembly member Colm Gildernew said Lisnahull is a "very close community" and that people in the area would reach out to those affected to support them.

"These incidents are dreadful anywhere they happen, it has hit the town of Dungannon at this point in time and the community here will react and respond to that."

Sinn Féin councillor Deirdre Varsani said on Saturday that there was "huge shock" in the local community at what had happened.

She added there was "huge concern" for the families affected and for the injured child, adding that those impacted faced a "number of weeks and months" dealing with the trauma.

Varsani also urged people to avoid speculation, adding: "Your thoughts really should be with anybody who has been injured, anybody who witnessed it or anybody who has been impacted by it."

Independent councillor Barry Monteith said people in the area were "dismayed".

He said the community would have to "support people the best they can" in the aftermath of the incident.

Monteith also called for a "little bit of restraint until the proper facts emerge", adding that rumours and speculation on social media did not help grieving families or those coming to terms with what had happened.

Alliance Party assembly member Connie Egan said it was "incredibly distressing and shocking news".

"My thoughts are with everyone affected, especially the child who has sadly been injured. I wish them a full recovery.

"I would urge people to follow the advice of the PSNI while the investigation continues and to avoid the area, and to please refrain from any speculation during this very difficult time."

articles.title: Bath photography exhibition shows 'spirit' of mixed ability rugby
articles.summary: The free exhibition at Bath Central Library features images from Bath Mixed Ability Rugby.
articles.body:
A new photographic exhibition celebrates a rugby club for players of all abilities, from those with disabilities to former players.

Bath Mixed Ability Rugby formed last year when two mixed ability rugby clubs, Walcott Warriors and Stothert & Pitt, merged and players train at a rugby ground in Bristol Road, Bath.

The free exhibition at Bath Central Library features images by photographer Jon Taylor and runs until 27 September.

It aims to capture what Taylor called "the spirit of the club - training sessions in all weathers and players supporting and learning from one another".

Farmers call for food rules update after heatwaves

How rail chiefs hope to make line more reliable after 'appalling' summer

The younger record fans turning to older vinyl

Jude Watson, 24, who is autistic and has a learning disability, said he never misses a session and is inseparable from his friend Jamie, who also plays at the club.

"I really like playing rugby with my friend Jamie," he said.

"I do lots of running which makes me feel good and I can catch the ball even when it's moving fast.

"The best part is when we hold arms in a circle at the end of training and do lots of cheering."

The club is also a refuge for former club rugby players who can no longer take part in regular games because of injury.

Alex Peters played rugby union in school, university and club teams, but a serious shoulder injury ended his playing days.

"It's just a phenomenal environment where you have the most kind of unlikely friendships forming which are just beautiful to see," he said.

"What's surprised me, personally, is seeing some of the development of the guys who wouldn't want to lie on the ground, for example, or they might have been afraid of trying to catch a ball.

"To see the developments for those individuals has been fantastic.

"It's just one of the beautiful things about rugby in its purest sense - that everyone's equal on the pitch having a wonderful time together."

Club coach Dave Copeland said: "Every training session involves someone doing something you would never have imagined them doing when they first joined the club.

"Every training session involves incredible laughter and humour - and every session you get to see players developing as rugby players, as friends of each other and as individuals.

articles.title: Niger’s military-led government says it contained mutiny: What next?
articles.summary: Mutiny began at a military base in Niamey and spread to area near the presidential palace and state broadcaster.
articles.body:
In the latest turmoil to hit Niger in West Africa, the military-led government says it has contained a mutiny in the capital, Niamey, after hours of gunfire and explosions near key military and government sites.

A military base at Diori Hamani International Airport was first targeted on Saturday by renegade soldiers, followed by attacks on the state broadcaster and presidential palace.

State TV said security forces gradually regained control, while dozens of rebel soldiers were reportedly killed or arrested.

The mutiny is another blow to Niger’s military leadership, which has failed to bring stability to the country since it took over in a coup three years ago. Since then, the military ruler and President General Abdourahamane Tchiani has pivoted the country away from the West, including its former colonial ruler, France.

He has forged close security ties with Russia in efforts to tackle the growing threat from armed groups, but that has not deterred fighters linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS) from mounting attacks.

So what happened, who was behind the mutiny and what does it mean for Niger’s military government?

The attacks started shortly after midnight on Saturday at Base 101, a major military facility inside Niamey’s international airport complex previously used by US forces.

General Salifou Mody, Niger’s defence minister, said a group of soldiers detained some of their comrades and opened fire at “certain sensitive sites” in the capital.

The fighting lasted for several hours, during which the state broadcaster was temporarily taken off air, while gunfire and explosions were reported around the airport and presidential palace.

Authorities said security forces responded quickly and helped regain control. The ruling military council, known as the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland, urged people to remain calm.

“Our Defence and Security Forces are mobilised for the Defence of the Fatherland. Let us remain united, vigilant and supportive,” it said.

By late Saturday, military authorities and state TV said the mutiny had been contained. Dozens of soldiers had been killed or arrested. Africa Corps, the Kremlin-backed force, received a request for assistance in neutralising the mutineers in the capital, said Viktor Voropaev, the Russian ambassador to Niger, in an interview with TASS news agency on Saturday.

Africa Corps is a Russian state-controlled paramilitary organisation established by the Russian Ministry of Defence, replacing and absorbing the African operations of the privately -run Russian militia, the Wagner Group.

The whereabouts of military leader Tchiani have not been confirmed.

Base 101 houses the general staff of the unified force of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), which includes Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso. The AES was established in 2023 to combat armed rebellion in the Sahel region.

It also houses the headquarters of the Africa Corps, which supports Sahel states in combating armed groups.

Who were the renegade soldiers behind the mutiny?

The mutineers appear to have included young soldiers from areas outside Niamey, particularly the southwest of Niger.

Reuters news agency reported that the operation involved soldiers from Ouallam, Tera and Dosso, citing analysts and security officials. Troops from those areas have suffered heavy losses fighting armed groups, particularly the regional ISIL affiliate.

The exact size of the mutinous force, and who led the mutiny, was not immediately clear. But analysts said the involvement of frontline troops points to growing frustration within the military.

“These mass-casualty overrun attacks on the Nigerien military are becoming commonplace and will continue to fuel unrest and aggravate tensions within the army ranks,” said Heni Nsaibia, senior West Africa analyst at Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED).

July 2023 – Niger’s military government seized power in a coup, saying the elected government had failed to contain armed groups.

August 2023 : Regional bloc ECOWAS imposes sanctions and threatens military intervention; Tchiani proposes a three-year transition.

September 2023 : Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso establish the Alliance of Sahel States (AES). France agrees to withdraw its ambassador and 1,500 troops.

January 2024: Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso announce their withdrawal from ECOWAS.

June 2024: An attack in western Niger kills 20 soldiers and a civilian, one of the deadliest assaults on the military since the coup.

September 2024: Niger suspends its military pact with the US. Washington subsequently withdraws its troops and closes its two bases – Air Base 101 in Niamey and Air Base 201 near the northern city of Agadez. Built at a cost of more than $100m, Air Base 201 was used for manned and drone surveillance flights and other operations in efforts to target ISIL fighters and Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a regional affiliate of al-Qaeda.

October 2025: Kevin Rideout, a pilot with the evangelical missionary agency SIM International, was abducted in Niamey.

January 2026: ISIL claims responsibility for an attack on an air force base at Niger’s Diori Hamani International Airport and the adjoining military base in Niamey.

June 2026: An armed attack on Niamey airport kills 11 soldiers and two civilians.

August 29, 2026: Soldiers mutiny at Niamey’s Base 101, with gunfire around the airport, presidential palace and other sensitive sites.

Niger’s military invoked increasing armed violence to seize power in the 2023 coup. It accused the elected government of failing to quash armed rebellion.

However, three years later, armed groups remain a major threat – fighters affiliated with al-Qaeda and ISIL have continued to carry out attacks.

The military-led government boosted its ties with Russia as Niger told France and the US to withdraw their forces. Niger has also joined Burkina Faso and Mali in the AES in order to put up a united fight against armed groups.

Nevertheless, the shift has not stopped unrest. The repeated attacks and heavy military casualties have fuelled frustration among frontline troops.

ACLED’s Nsaibia described the mutiny as a sign of a wider problem.

“Deteriorating insecurity drove the coups that swept across the central Sahel and the latest events show how these same pressures are now fuelling unrest within the militaries that seized power,” he said.

What has been the response of the international community?

The AES expressed support for Niger’s military leadership, saying in a statement that the mutineers had been “contained and thwarted”, calling the mutiny a “betrayal by a group of soldiers involved in a destabilisation plot”.

It was unclear whether Mali or Burkina Faso provided direct military assistance to their ally.

Algeria condemned the events and expressed its “full solidarity and firm support” for Niger.

Turkiye’s foreign ministry called for restraint and posted on X that it hoped “calm would be restored as soon as possible” while pledging to continue supporting Niger.

Why did the attack happen and what comes next?

The mutiny “speaks of deeper institutional and structural challenges within the military”, Kabir Adamu, an Abuja-based security expert, told Al Jazeera.

There is an argument that “persons who have received significant training, both within and outside [the military] are now occupying political positions and are not in the front line where they are needed to address the complex security challenges facing the country”, he said.

There are also the issues of equipment, repository, rotation of military forces.

“The grievances grew to a point where this mutiny sort of occurred,” said Adamu, the managing director at Beacon Security Innovations, adding: “as part of that mutiny, based on the places they targeted, it was clearly an attempt to overthrow the government”.

“If [Tchiani] does not address the deep-rooted socioeconomic, cultural, environmental and security challenges that he promised when he took over power in July 2023, then those issues will continue to rear their head,” Adamu said.

articles.title: Harry and Meghan are back in Britain: Tracing their journey from royal fairytale to rupture
articles.summary: UK News: When Prince Harry and Meghan Markle married at St George’s Chapel in Windsor in May 2018, the moment seemed to carry more than the promise of a royal .
articles.body: When Prince Harry and Meghan Markle married at St George’s Chapel in Windsor in May 2018, the moment seemed to carry more than the promise of a royal romance.It looked, in many ways, like the beginning of a new era.There was the prince who had grown up in the glare of the British monarchy, and the American actress who had entered an institution built on centuries of tradition. There was the spectacle of the wedding, the crowds outside Windsor and the global attention that followed.And there was something else.Harry was the younger son of the future king. Meghan was an outsider who had married into the world's most famous royal family. Together, they appeared to offer the monarchy a different kind of future.For a time, the picture was almost perfect.Harry and Meghan joined Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, in what was widely seen as a younger royal generation capable of carrying the institution into the future. The four were often portrayed as the monarchy's modern "fab four".But the image did not last.Within less than two years, Harry and Meghan would announce that they were stepping back from their roles as senior working royals. They would leave Britain, first for Canada and then for California, and build a life outside the formal machinery of the monarchy.The years that followed would bring an explosive interview with Oprah Winfrey, a Netflix documentary, Harry's memoir and an increasingly public rupture between the Sussexes and other members of the Royal Family.The "fab four" became a symbol of what might have been.William and Catherine moved closer to the centre of the institution. Harry and Meghan moved further away. And yet, Britain never quite disappeared from their story.Harry has repeatedly returned to the country he once left. Family events, royal occasions and personal circumstances kept bringing him and Meghan back to Britain.Their latest return therefore raises a question that goes beyond where the Sussexes live.Can Harry and Meghan ever really leave Britain behind?Before Meghan, there was DianaHarry did not grow up with an ordinary understanding of what it meant to be royal.His childhood was lived inside one of the world's most scrutinised families. His parents' marriage was played out under extraordinary public attention. His mother became one of the most recognisable women on the planet.Diana's popularity was extraordinary, but so was the attention surrounding her.Her relationship with the monarchy, her marriage to then-Prince Charles, her separation and her life after the breakdown of the marriage all became subjects of intense media interest.For Harry, this was not merely history.It was his childhood.He was 12 when Diana died in a car crash in Paris on August 31, 1997. For Harry, her death defined the collision between the private lives of the Royal Family and the enormous appetite of the press and public for their stories.That history matters when looking at Harry's relationship with Meghan.Meghan was not Diana. Her experience was not Diana's, but there was an undeniable echo.Like Diana, Meghan became an extraordinarily prominent woman after marrying into the British Royal Family. Like Diana, she attracted intense media attention. And like Diana, her relationship with the institution became the subject of relentless public discussion.For Harry, however, the connection was even more personal.He had already spent his childhood watching his mother struggle with the pressures of royal life and media scrutiny. But with Meghan, Harry was no longer the boy being carried behind his mother's funeral procession.He was the husband. And his response to the press became increasingly forceful.Harry's hostility towards sections of the media is not a mere disagreement over headlines. It is also rooted in a childhood experience that shaped his understanding of what publicity can do to a royal family.In that sense, Meghan's arrival brought the concerns back into Harry’s adult life.2018: The couple who could have changed the monarchyThe wedding at Windsor seemed to suggest that the institution had found a way to embrace change without abandoning tradition.Meghan's background made her different from many previous royal brides. She had already established herself as a public figure before entering the Royal Family.Harry and Meghan quickly developed their own charitable and public identity. Their tours generated huge interest. They appeared energetic, modern and comfortable with the global media spotlight.The Sussexes seemed capable of becoming an important bridge between the traditional institution and a younger, more diverse audience.And they were not alone. William and Catherine were also developing their own public roles.The four represented a generational shift.William was preparing for an eventual role as King. Harry was the popular younger brother with a strong connection to younger audiences. Catherine had become one of the most recognisable members of the Royal Family. Meghan brought a distinctly international profile.The monarchy appeared to have a formidable younger team.The "fab four" were not a formal royal institution or constitutional arrangement. It was a media description of a family dynamic and public image.But the image mattered.It suggested unity, continuity, and the difficult experiences of the previous generation could perhaps be left behind.2019: When the fairytale began to frayThe Sussexes' first years as working royals were accompanied by intense media interest.The birth of their son Archie in May 2019 brought another moment of global attention. But by then, the couple's relationship with the British press had become increasingly difficult.Harry and Meghan's approach to privacy was also markedly different from the traditional expectations surrounding royal life.This was not simply a question of wanting to avoid cameras.Royal life operates on an unusual bargain. Members of the Royal Family receive enormous public attention and occupy privileged positions within a national institution, but they are also expected to undertake public duties and accept a degree of scrutiny.The Sussexes increasingly appeared uncomfortable with that bargain.\Their decision to establish a separate household and their increasingly independent public identity were signs of a relationship with the institution that was changing.2020: Megxit - the announcement that altered everythingIn January 2020, Harry and Meghan announced that they would step back as senior members of the Royal Family and work towards becoming financially independent.The phrase "Megxit" soon became a shorthand for the decision, although the reality was more than a couple moving house.Harry and Meghan were stepping away from the traditional role of senior working royals.The distinction is important.Being a member of the Royal Family is not necessarily the same as being a working member of it. The monarchy includes relatives who do not undertake official duties on behalf of the monarch. Working royals, by contrast, represent the King and carry out engagements and responsibilities connected to the institution.Harry and Meghan were choosing the second path.They wanted greater control over their lives and financial independence while retaining their family connection and royal identities, and the eventual destination was California.From royal duty to a life of their ownCalifornia changed the Sussexes' relationship with the public.In Britain, Harry and Meghan had been members of a constitutional institution.In America, they became a global couple building an independent public brand.They signed commercial deals. They developed media projects. They spoke publicly about their experiences.Their story was no longer being told primarily through royal announcements.They were increasingly telling it themselves, and that was where the next great rupture began.Oprah: when the palace walls became transparentIn March 2021, Harry and Meghan's interview with Oprah Winfrey became a global media event.The couple discussed their experiences within the Royal Family and made serious allegations about their treatment and the pressures surrounding Meghan's life as a royal.The significance went beyond any individual claim.For generations, the British monarchy had operated according to an unwritten principle of restraint. Private family disagreements were generally kept private.Harry and Meghan broke with that tradition.The Sussexes had their own account of what had happened.The institution did not respond with an equivalent public narrative.The result was a new kind of royal conflict: one side speaking openly, the other largely maintaining institutional silence.The family dispute had become a global media story.And the "fab four" image was becoming increasingly difficult to remember.The Queen's death and the return to BritainIn September 2022, Queen Elizabeth II died.For Harry, the event brought him back into a world from which he had deliberately created distance.The death of his grandmother placed family, monarchy and personal history in the same physical space.Harry returned to Britain at a moment when the institution itself was changing.Charles became King Charles III.William became heir to the throne.The Royal Family entered a new reign.The monarchy that Harry had left behind in 2020 had changed.But so had Harry. He was no longer simply the younger prince standing behind his brother. He was a husband and father living in California, a bestselling author and an internationally prominent figure who had publicly discussed his relationship with the Royal Family.Yet, in Britain, he was still Harry, Diana’s younger son and William's little brother.Spare and the collapse of the brothers' old imageIf Oprah had opened the door, Harry's memoir Spare pushed it much further.Published in 2023, the book offered Harry's most detailed account of his life inside the Royal Family and his relationship with William.The title itself was loaded with meaning.Harry had grown up knowing that William was the heir to the throne, and he was the "spare".The memoir made the distance between the brothers one of the defining narratives of the modern monarchy.The old image of William and Harry as inseparable brothers had been replaced by something far more complicated.The “fab four” split paths. William and Catherine remained inside, Harry and Meghan remained outside.The Diana parallel becomes harder to ignoreDiana's story had demonstrated that a royal could become bigger than the institution itself.Her popularity was extraordinary. Her public identity could not easily be contained within the formal boundaries of royal duty.Harry and Meghan's story is different, but it raises a related question.What happens when members of the Royal Family become global public figures with audiences and platforms independent of the institution?Diana eventually left the formal structure of the monarchy after her divorce from Charles, but remained one of the world's most famous women.Harry and Meghan made a different choice.They left royal duties while retaining their titles and global profile, and they established a life independent of the British monarchy.The parallel should not be overstated.Diana's circumstances were unique. Meghan's were different. Their marriages, departures and public lives unfolded in different eras. However, the picture also paints the difficulty of separating the individual from the institution once that individual has become globally famous.For Harry, the connection is even more profound.He has spent much of his adult life trying to protect his private life from the kind of media attention that surrounded his mother. And every time he returns to Britain, he returns not simply to a country, but to the landscape of his childhood.Why Britain keeps pulling Harry backHarry's life in California is now established. Yet Britain continues to draw him back.Some returns have been unavoidable consequences of family events. Others have been connected to personal matters and his continuing relationship with the country.That repeated movement across the Atlantic is revealing.Harry may have left the institution and royal duties. But he cannot leave his history behind.Britain is his childhood. It is where his mother became one of the most famous women in the world. It is also where he served in the British Army, married Meghan, and where his relationship with his family was formed long before the public became aware of the fractures within it.For Meghan, Britain carries a different meaning. Her relationship with Britain was created through Harry and the monarchy.For their children, the connection is still more complicated.Archie and Lilibet are growing up primarily in the United States. Their father's childhood in Britain is part of their family history rather than their everyday experience.The Sussex family's future therefore raises another question.Will Britain remain a place of family obligation and royal history, or can it become something more personal for the next generation?A monarchy that moved onThere is another reason the Sussexes' return feels different today.The monarchy moved on.Queen Elizabeth II died and King Charles III began a new reign. The Sussexes, meanwhile, have created a parallel life.That does not necessarily mean that every return to Britain represents reconciliation.Nor does it mean that Harry and Meghan are preparing to resume their old roles.The institutional distinction remains important: a return to Britain is not automatically a return to royal duty.A family visit is not the same as becoming a working royal again.The long road homeIn 2018, Harry and Meghan's wedding looked like a beginning. But it was also the beginning of a chain of events that would reshape the modern British monarchy.The couple who were expected to help refresh the institution eventually walked away from it.The "fab four" who appeared to embody a united younger generation became two very different couples pursuing very different lives.And Harry, the boy who lost his mother under the most intense glare of the world's media, became an adult determined to control the way his own family was exposed to that same glare.The Sussexes may have left royal life.But Harry cannot leave behind the country that shaped him, the family into which he was born or the memory of the mother whose own complicated relationship with the monarchy continues to cast a long shadow over his story.Eight years after the wedding, the Sussexes stand outside the royal future. But they are not entirely detached from it either.Perhaps that is the enduring paradox of Harry and Meghan's journey.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 2 dead, 9 hurt in Trenton mass shooting
articles.summary: Two people were killed and nine have been hospitalized after police say gunfire erupted at a gathering that may have been a cookout in Trenton, New Jersey, overnight.
articles.body: Two people were killed and nine have been hospitalized after police say gunfire erupted at a gathering that may have been a cookout in Trenton, New Jersey, overnight. Capt. David Ordille of the Trenton Police Department said the shooting happened at around 12:25 a.m. along the 100 block of Locust Street in Trenton, New Jersey. Eleven people were shot, he said. Early Sunday morning, police had taped off an entrance to Capital Health Regional Medical Center, about two miles away from the shooting, and a vehicle that was parked at an emergency room entrance was seen being towed away. The vehicle had visible damage. Outside the medical center, NBC10’s Katy Zachry spoke to a woman who said her nephew was brought to the hospital after having been shot in the head. Family and friends of victims who have spoken to NBC10 said that before the incident, people had gotten together for a neighborhood gathering and a cookout. Then, at some point, the shooting started. A woman who told NBC10 she was at the cookout but asked to remain anonymous said about 150 people were at the event when they first heard shots. She said the crowd thought the shooting was over after an initial volley of shots, before it erupted again. However, she said she did not know how many people were firing. At the scene early Sunday, investigators were seen placing nearly 40 evidence markers along the ground. Police have not yet detailed how this incident unfolded and have not provided further information on any suspects in this case. An investigation is ongoing.

articles.title: In 1966, Marlon Brando bought a private Polynesian atoll after filming ‘Mutiny on the Bounty’; it is now a wildlife sanctuary where 15,614 green turtle hatchlings emerged in one season
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A private Pacific atoll once owned by Hollywood actor Marlon Brando has become one of French Polynesia’s most important marine conservation sites, wit.
articles.body: A private Pacific atoll once owned by Hollywood actor Marlon Brando has become one of French Polynesia’s most important marine conservation sites, with thousands of sea turtle hatchlings recorded after decades of habitat protection. Biologists monitoring Tetiaroa Atoll recorded more than 15,614 green sea turtle hatchlings emerging from nests during one recent monitoring season, according to figures published by conservation group Tetiaroa Society and research partner Te mana o te moana. The annual survey runs from September to March and recorded 113 nesting females and about 161 nests spread across the atoll’s protected coral islets. The success seen today is the result of a major environmental transformation that began six decades ago in the South Pacific.From Hollywood set to private sanctuaryBrando first visited Tetiaroa in 1960 while looking for filming locations for the MGM historical drama Mutiny on the Bounty. He was fascinated by the quiet group of 12 small islets surrounding a clear turquoise lagoon. In 1966, he negotiated the purchase of the atoll’s land rights from descendants of American dentist Johnston Walter Williams. In his 1994 autobiography, Songs My Mother Taught Me, Brando remembered arriving on a local fishing boat and described the remote atoll as "more gorgeous than anything I had anticipated". Instead of turning the land into a large commercial resort, Brando wanted Tetiaroa to remain isolated and protected from heavy development. He built a simple village on Motu Onetahi for his family and visiting scientists, creating the early foundation for long-term conservation and the protection of native Pacific wildlife.Research and invasive species controlAfter Brando died in 2004, his estate worked with Pacific Beachcomber to continue his environmental vision. Together, they helped establish the Tetiaroa Society, an organisation focused on scientific research, Indigenous cultural preservation and environmental protection across tropical island ecosystems. Research teams operate from the Ecostation on Motu Onetahi, where scientists from different countries study coral reef health, ocean acidification and native plants. One of the most important steps in restoring the islands was removing introduced predators that threatened ground-nesting seabirds and sea turtle nests. According to project information from the Tetiaroa Society and international partner Island Conservation, targeted programmes successfully removed invasive Pacific rats from islets including Reiono and Rimatuu. With the rats gone, native plants and animals were able to recover with fewer threats. At the same time, teams working with the Louis Malardé Institute in Tahiti have tested ways to control mosquitoes without using chemical pesticides that could harm the surrounding marine environment.Long-term sea turtle monitoringThe green sea turtle, known locally in Tahitian as honu, depends heavily on Tetiaroa’s quiet beaches for breeding. Female turtles usually return to the same beaches where they were born 25 to 30 years earlier, using ocean currents and Earth’s magnetic field to find their way back.Data collected by marine biology team Te mana o te moana shows how closely the turtles are monitored:Biologists recorded more than 430 separate turtle crawls along the atoll’s beaches during the latest survey.Researchers identified 113 individual females coming ashore to lay eggs.Field teams monitored 161 nests and estimated hatchling numbers by carefully counting the empty eggshells left behind after the young turtles emerged.An estimated 15,614 hatchlings successfully made it to the water.Protection efforts cover the entire nesting process. Patrol teams check beaches at night when females come ashore, tag adult turtles to follow their nesting patterns over several years and protect nests from flooding and any remaining predators.Eco-tourism helps fund conservationTetiaroa’s conservation work is supported by a self-sustaining financial system centred on The Brando, a luxury eco-resort on Motu Onetahi. The resort uses several environmental technologies, including a Sea Water Air Conditioning system that pumps cold ocean water from a depth of 930 metres to cool buildings while reducing electricity use. Money generated from guests staying at the resort helps pay for the boats, equipment, laboratory facilities and other support needed by the Tetiaroa Society. According to the society’s strategic updates, its wider goal is to show that luxury tourism, scientific research and Indigenous Polynesian leadership can work together to protect fragile island ecosystems.Threats beyond the protected lagoonAlthough Tetiaroa’s nesting beaches remain protected, marine biologists warn that green turtles still face serious dangers once they leave the lagoon. Satellite tracking has shown that after the breeding season ends in April, female turtles can travel thousands of miles across the open ocean to reach feeding grounds, including seagrass meadows around Fiji. During these journeys, they face threats from industrial longline fishing equipment, swallowing marine plastic and warmer ocean temperatures. Rising temperatures can also change beach sand temperatures, which is important because temperature affects the sex of developing turtle embryos. Conservationists say keeping nesting beaches such as Tetiaroa safe and free of invasive predators gives Pacific green turtles an important advantage. High numbers of hatchlings can help make up for the many young turtles lost during their lives at sea. The successful emergence of more than 15,000 young turtles in one season shows the lasting impact of a protected sanctuary first established six decades ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Man posed as San Francisco 49er to defraud women of $1.3 million
articles.summary: A man was accused of pretending to be a San Francisco 49ers player to defraud women, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Oregon.
articles.body: A man was accused of pretending to be a San Francisco 49ers player to defraud women, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Oregon. Beginning in February 2022, Daejon Labrayae Love, 35, and Taylor Jamie Chan, 18, created fictitious investments to defraud numerous women in Oregon, Washington, Idaho and California, according to court documents. Authorities said both men were arrested when Chan flew from California on Monday to meet Love in Boise, Idaho. Both were charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud. Love would meet most of the women through dating apps and pretend to have a lavish lifestyle on social media, falsely portraying himself as a 49ers player or a wealthy real estate investor, according to authorities. The attorney’s office said Love convinced victims they were in sincere romantic relationships with him, that he was a sophisticated investor and that Chan was his “investment adviser,” who helped Love to grow a fortune of tens of millions of dollars. Love told the victims he wanted to build wealth and a future with them, authorities said. Officials added Love advertised nonexistent investment vehicles, claiming these investments would generate massive returns for both him and his victims. Court documents said Love used phone apps to create fictitious bank and investment accounts and balances to show the victims and make the scheme appear legitimate. Authorities said Love and Chan exchanged electronic communications in which Chan pretended to be Love’s investment adviser and would send messages encouraging Love to invest in new opportunities. Love would then send screenshots of those messages to the victims to convince them to send money to either of them, according to court documents. The U.S. attorney’s office said the pair would have video calls with the victims to show them falsified investment gains and encourage them to part with their money. If the victims did not have money, authorities said, Love sometimes instructed them to take a loan; if they were left with no more money to invest or asked too many questions, Love would block them, stop any communication with them and keep the money. Financial records show the pair received about $1.3 million from victims, according to authorities. Officials said 26 victims have been identified, but the FBI believes there could be more. The FBI encourages anyone with information on Love or Chan to submit a tip at the FBI website or to call 1-800-CALL-FBI.
